item.title: Microsoft Entra MFA Changes, Phishing Kits, OAuth Spoofing, and SAP Critical Flaws
item.content:encoded:
OAuth Client ID Spoofing Lets Attackers Validate Stolen Microsoft Entra Credentials — Must Read

Proofpoint says threat actors are abusing OAuth client ID spoofing in Microsoft Entra ID to enumerate accounts and validate stolen passwords without generating normal successful sign-in telemetry. The technique fragments attempts across fake application IDs, helping campaigns targeting millions of users evade application-based detections, rate limits, and some Conditional Access policies.

  • Proofpoint said at least two threat actors are using OAuth client ID spoofing in cloud campaigns to enumerate Microsoft Entra ID user accounts and validate stolen credentials without generating successful sign-in events.
  • The technique uses spoofed client IDs in HTTP POST requests to Microsoft’s OAuth 2.0 token endpoint with the Resource Owner Password Credentials flow, allowing attackers to infer account and password validity from AADSTS error responses.
  • When a spoofed client ID is used, Entra sign-in logs record only the application ID without a corresponding application name, which can cause detections based on specific application names to miss the activity.
  • Proofpoint identified UNK_pyreq2323 as targeting more than 1 million accounts across nearly 4,000 tenants from AWS infrastructure between January and March 2026, causing lockouts for roughly 28% of targeted users.
  • Proofpoint identified UNK_OutFlareAZ as starting in December 2025 and using Cloudflare infrastructure to target over 2 million users with 3.7 million randomized spoofed application IDs.

SAP warns of critical flaws in NetWeaver and Commerce Cloud — Must Read

SAP’s July 2026 security updates fix 16 vulnerabilities, including three critical flaws in NetWeaver AS ABAP, SAP Approuter, and SAP Commerce Cloud that could enable data access, modification, denial of service, or abuse of default credentials. SAP says it has not seen evidence of exploitation yet, but customers should patch promptly.

  • SAP addressed 16 vulnerabilities across multiple products in its July 2026 security updates, including three critical flaws in NetWeaver, Commerce Cloud, and AppRouter.
  • CVE-2026-44747 is a critical memory corruption issue in SAP NetWeaver Application Server ABAP caused by an out-of-bounds write weakness that could affect confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
  • CVE-2026-27690 is a critical HTTP Request Smuggling vulnerability in SAP Approuter that unauthenticated attackers can exploit with specially crafted HTTP requests to access user responses and trigger denial-of-service attacks.
  • CVE-2026-44761 is a critical SAP Commerce Cloud flaw caused by default credentials that can let attackers obtain valid access tokens and read or modify data through certain APIs.
  • SAP says it has not found evidence that the vulnerabilities patched in the July 2026 updates have been exploited in attacks.

11 Old Microsoft-Signed Linux UEFI Shims Could Let Attackers Bypass Secure Boot — Should Read

Researchers found 11 old Microsoft-signed Linux UEFI shim bootloaders that can still be abused to bypass Secure Boot and run malicious code before the operating system starts. Microsoft has revoked the affected shims, but systems remain at risk if revocation updates are not applied.

  • Cybersecurity researchers discovered 11 old Microsoft-signed UEFI shim applications that could be abused to bypass Secure Boot on most systems using UEFI.
  • The vulnerable shim bootloaders expose any UEFI-based machine that trusts Microsoft’s “Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011” third-party UEFI certificate authority certificate, regardless of the installed operating system.
  • An attacker with administrative privileges or the ability to modify the boot process could use the affected shims to execute arbitrary code before the operating system loads.
  • Microsoft revoked the impacted shim bootloaders as part of its June 2026 Patch Tuesday update following responsible disclosure to the company in February.
  • ESET warned that expiration of the Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 certificate does not affect Secure Boot verification unless bootloaders signed with the expired certificate are explicitly revoked by hash.

New phishing kits target Microsoft 365 accounts, evade MFA — Should Read

Two new phishing kits, Jalisco and OmegaLord, are targeting Microsoft 365 accounts with methods designed to bypass MFA, including real-time device-code phishing and harvesting phone numbers alongside credentials. ReliaQuest recommends restricting device-code authentication and tightening device registration limits to reduce account takeover risk.

  • ReliaQuest researchers discovered two phishing kits, Jalisco and OmegaLord, being used to target Microsoft 365 accounts and evade multi-factor authentication.
  • Jalisco uses device-code phishing by generating fresh Microsoft OAuth device codes when victims open the phishing page, allowing attackers to authorize attacker-controlled devices without needing the victim’s username or password.
  • ReliaQuest observed attackers registering multiple rogue devices on compromised accounts, sometimes using names containing “Microsoft” or “Windows” to appear less suspicious.
  • After compromising accounts, attackers search SharePoint and other SaaS services for valuable data, exfiltrate it in as little as six minutes, and follow up with extortion demands.
  • OmegaLord uses a fake PDF Reader login page to steal email addresses, passwords, and phone numbers, which could help attackers bypass MFA protections.

Microsoft Entra ID gets passkeys default authentication starting September — Should Read

Microsoft will make passkeys the default authentication method for Entra ID starting in September 2026 and will retire native SMS and voice MFA on February 1, 2027. Organizations should move users to phishing-resistant authentication methods to avoid sign-in disruptions and reduce credential theft risk.

  • Microsoft announced that passkeys will become the default authentication method for the Entra ID enterprise identity service starting in September 2026.
  • Entra ID users who currently use phone-based SMS or voice authentication will be automatically enabled for passkeys and prompted to register one the next time they perform multifactor authentication.
  • Microsoft will retire Microsoft-provided telecom delivery for SMS and voice authentication on February 1, 2027, and will no longer offer SMS and voice as a native Microsoft Entra capability.
  • Users already signing in with passkeys, Windows Hello for Business, FIDO2 security keys, smart cards, or other phishing-resistant methods will be able to continue using those methods.
  • Microsoft said organizations should ensure all users move to phishing-resistant authentication before the SMS and voice retirement date to avoid sign-in disruptions.

Study of 85 Crypto Wallet Extensions Finds Address Leaks and Cross-Site Tracking Risks — Should Read

KU Leuven researchers found that many popular crypto wallet browser extensions leak wallet addresses in ways that can link a user’s separate addresses, persist after logout, and enable cross-site tracking or real-world identity matching. The issue is largely built into how wallets interact with websites, and several major wallet vendors declined to treat it as a serious bug.

  • KU Leuven researchers tested 85 popular crypto wallet browser extensions with about 35 million Chrome Web Store users and found privacy weaknesses that can link and track the people using them.
  • Seventeen wallets exposed connections between a user’s separate wallet addresses, either by bundling multiple addresses into one server request or by sending separate requests within milliseconds of each other.
  • Thirty-six of the 85 wallets announce themselves to any page they load, creating an installed-wallet fingerprint that works even if the user never connects a wallet and blocks cookies.
  • In 22 of those 36 wallets, a site could still read the user’s address after asking the wallet to revoke access, with that access surviving cookie clearing and browser restarts.
  • The researchers reported the cross-site issue to affected wallet makers, but several vendors declined to treat it as a bug, while Coinbase Wallet, Coin98, and Hana Wallet fixed it.

A Fake Malwarebytes Renewal, Signed by Google — Should Read

A fake Malwarebytes renewal invoice was sent via a legitimate Google Calendar invite from a newly registered Google Workspace domain, using phone numbers instead of malicious links or files to push a vishing scam. Because Google signed the message and all links were legitimate, detection depended on behavioral signals like the unknown organizer domain, brand mismatch, callback numbers, and user reporting.

  • An attacker registered betskl[.]com, created a Google Workspace account on it, and used Google Calendar to send a fake Malwarebytes Security Operations renewal invoice to a senior executive at a hospitality company.
  • The calendar invite claimed a $598.75 four-year Malwarebytes Premium Family Plan charge and provided two phone numbers for the recipient to call to dispute the supposed unauthorized charge.
  • The message contained no malicious links or code-bearing attachment, because its links resolved to calendar.google.com and the invite.ics attachment was a plain Google-generated iCalendar file.
  • DKIM and composite authentication passed because Google sent and signed the message, while the organizer address was an unrelated newly registered domain with no SPF or DMARC records.
  • The executive reported the message as an unknown sender, Themis identified it as suspicious vishing targeting a VIP recipient, and the message was quarantined and permanently deleted.

J-Space: The Logs AI Security Has Never Had — May Read

Anthropic’s J-space research suggests AI agents may have an internal “intent” signal that can reveal deception, prompt injection awareness, or manipulation before actions occur. The key takeaway is that frontier labs should expose this workspace telemetry to enterprise security teams as a new class of logs for detecting and responding to agentic AI risks.

  • Anthropic published interpretability research describing a small internal structure in Claude called the J-space, which the article says acts like a mental workspace for deliberate multi-step reasoning.
  • The article says the J-lens technique can read the J-space by identifying words associated with internal activity patterns, including concepts that may not appear in the model’s output.
  • In Anthropic’s examples, words such as “ERROR,” “injection,” “fake,” “manipulation,” “secretly,” “deliberately,” and “fraud” appeared in the J-space during scenarios involving bugs, prompt injection, staged tests, falsified scores, or sabotage-trained models.
  • The article argues that J-space telemetry would add a third layer of AI agent monitoring beyond what an agent says and what it does, potentially helping teams correlate internal signals with actions like file writes or external content consumption.
  • The article calls on Anthropic and other frontier labs to expose workspace telemetry to enterprise customers, while noting objections such as model intellectual property, compute cost, adversarial evasion, and false positives.

The serpent’s tongue: Luring the Python out of its den — Optional

Python packages can execute malicious code during installation or later through abused features like setup.py hooks, .pth files, sitecustomize modules, PYTHONPATH changes, entry points, and import-time payloads. Developers should reduce supply-chain risk with dependency auditing, pinned versions and hashes, isolated builds, cooldown periods for new releases, and SBOM/trusted publishing practices.

  • Python’s readable syntax, broad capabilities, and extensive package ecosystem make it an attractive target for malicious packages and supply-chain attacks.
  • A Python package can execute malicious code simply during installation, without requiring the victim to import the package, run its entry point, or otherwise interact with the infected code.
  • The article groups malicious Python package techniques into build hook abuses, such as setup.py command classes, .pth files, site hook modules, and PYTHONPATH manipulation, and package content abuses, such as import-time payloads, __main__.py scripts, entry point hijacking, and overriding legitimate package contents.
  • Persistent techniques described in the article include .pth files and sitecustomize or usercustomize hooks, which can run payloads every time Python is invoked in the affected environment.
  • Recommended defenses include scanning packages with tools such as pip-audit, using lock files and cryptographic hashes, installing packages in isolated environments, applying dependency cooldowns, generating SBOMs, and using PyPI Trusted Publishing.

The State of Enterprise Cyber Crisis Readiness (report) — Optional

A global survey of 1,000 organizations found that while many have cyber incident response plans and run exercises, most still face major blockers because teams are not practicing and coordinating holistically. The key gap is cross-team communication and coordination, not simply a lack of staffing.

  • The report is based on a global study of 1,000 organizations across the US, UK, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region.
  • The study found a disconnect between organizations’ perceived cyber crisis readiness and their actual performance in cyber crisis response.
  • Ninety percent of organizations reported serious blockers to effective cyber response.
  • Less than 50% of organizations conduct tabletop exercises that include all the teams commonly involved in an actual crisis.
  • Seventy-one percent of organizations experienced at least one high-impact cyber incident that disrupted critical business functions in the past year, and 36% suffered multiple damaging incidents.

Human Risk Management 90-Day Playbook — Optional

Living Security’s 90-Day Human Risk Management Playbook outlines a data-driven approach for moving beyond generic security awareness training to identify high-risk employees and deliver targeted microlearning. It promises measurable improvements such as fewer repeat phishing clickers and higher reporting rates within one quarter.

  • Living Security, a Health-ISAC Community Champion, released a 90-Day Human Risk Management Playbook.
  • The article says most awareness programs are stuck in a compliance loop and see only 12% of actual human risk.
  • The playbook provides a modular, outcome-oriented roadmap for turning generic training into a data-driven engine for risk reduction.
  • The playbook describes how to identify the riskiest 10% of the workforce and automate targeted microlearning.
  • The article says the playbook can support measurable wins such as cutting repeat clickers by 40% and increasing report rates by 15% in one quarter.

Varonis Atlas Extends Coverage Across the Claude Enterprise Suite — From Claude Cowork to Claude Code — Optional

Varonis announced that its Atlas AI Security Platform now covers the full Claude enterprise suite, adding support for Claude Code and Claude Cowork alongside existing Claude Enterprise and Platform coverage. The update gives security teams runtime guardrails, monitoring, investigation, and posture management across Anthropic’s increasingly agentic tools.

  • Varonis Atlas now secures the entire Claude enterprise suite, extending existing support for Claude Enterprise and Claude Platform to Claude Code and Claude Cowork.
  • The article says Anthropic’s agents have expanded from answering questions to taking actions such as writing to local files, running terminal commands, and editing code.
  • For Claude Code, Atlas provides runtime guardrails, AI Detection and Response, AI Security Posture Management, and activity monitoring across prompts, LLM calls, tool calls, MCP interactions, command execution, and agent actions.
  • For Claude Cowork, Atlas supports a dedicated runtime integration that sends Cowork activity to Atlas so policies can evaluate events as they happen and apply separate policies, logging, and audit trails from Claude Code.
  • Varonis says comprehensive coverage means visibility follows Anthropic’s agents across Claude surfaces and connects back to the data context, permissions, and risk signals in the Varonis Data Security Platform.

How Pentera Turns AI Security Workflows into Validation Engines — Optional

Pentera is positioning its MCP Server as a way to feed validated attack-path evidence into AI security workflows, so AI assistants can prioritize and remediate risks based on what is actually exploitable rather than scanner severity alone. The key takeaway is that AI-driven security decisions become more reliable when grounded in continuous validation and re-testing.

  • The article argues that AI security workflows relying on fragmented risk signals cannot determine whether findings form real attack paths in an organization’s environment.
  • Pentera’s AI-powered security validation platform safely emulates real-world attack techniques against production environments to identify exposures that can actually be leveraged by an attacker.
  • Pentera’s validation results include evidence such as the technique used, systems reached, credentials obtained, privileges gained, assets at risk, and the objective achieved.
  • Pentera introduced an MCP Server that makes its validation data available to MCP-compatible AI assistants so teams can retrieve findings, review attack paths, access test results, and initiate validation activities using natural language.
  • Pentera’s MCP Server is described as running locally as a Docker container, using STDIO communication, opening no inbound ports, inheriting existing Pentera RBAC permissions, and logging interactions for auditability.

Microsoft starts testing cleaner Windows Search without ads — Optional

Microsoft is testing a cleaner Windows Search for Insiders that prioritizes relevant local results over ads and promotional suggestions, with clearer result sources and new controls for web and Store suggestions. The update also improves file/app search reliability, typo tolerance, and two-character file queries.

  • Microsoft is testing a cleaner and faster version of Windows Search that is intended to prioritize relevant results over ads and promotional content.
  • The Windows Search changes are available to Windows Insiders in the Experimental channel through Windows Search Box updates that began rolling out on Monday.
  • The rollout is being done through a Controlled Feature Rollout, so not all Insiders will see the new Windows Search immediately.
  • The updated Search results more clearly identify whether each result comes from an app, Windows setting, file, web result, or Microsoft Store suggestion.
  • Microsoft added a setting under Settings > Privacy & Security > Search that lets users choose whether Microsoft Store and web suggestions appear alongside local results.

[Video] Where protection starts: Cisco Talos Intelligence Integrations — Optional

Cisco is promoting its Talos Intelligence Integrations, which apply Talos threat intelligence across Cisco security and enterprise products to help identify and block malicious activity. The article points readers to a new video explaining how these integrations work and who builds them.

  • The article says cybersecurity teams often must make decisions with incomplete information while attackers benefit when defenders cannot see the full picture.
  • The article describes attackers using AI to rewrite malicious commands, malware that adapts its code upon installation, and models that can search old vulnerable code and exposed interfaces for exploitation opportunities.
  • Cisco Talos Intelligence Integrations are presented as helping answer questions such as whether a newly registered domain is part of an attack, whether an outbound connection is normal, or whether user behavior is unusual.
  • Talos reputation and detection integrations apply current threat intelligence across Cisco security and enterprise technologies to identify and block malicious activity.
  • The article introduces a new video featuring Talos personnel explaining how the integrations work and points readers to a more detailed overview on the Cisco Security website.
